implementation_notes: Go makes the split syntactic: a go statement executes a call in a new goroutine and returns immediately, so the asynchronous variant is an ordinary function that starts the work and returns a channel - `ch := make(chan Result, 1); go func() { ch <- f(ctx) }(); return ch` - and the collection step is a channel receive (or a select with ctx.Done() for the bounded wait). There is no Future type and deliberately no way to read a result other than receiving it, so hand-written handle/callback structures are un-idiomatic. For groups of tasks sync.WaitGroup counts completions, while golang.org/x/sync/errgroup adds the two things the pattern needs beyond counting: the first non-nil error is remembered and returned by Wait, and the group's derived context is cancelled as soon as one task fails - which is why the errgroup source treats error propagation and cancellation as part of the group, not of the individual call. Sending the outcome on a buffered channel also removes the classic requirement that the caller must be present before the call finishes.
pitfalls: An unbuffered channel with no reader leaks the goroutine forever; buffer by one or guarantee a receive.
A panic inside a goroutine is not recoverable by the caller and crashes the process: recover inside the goroutine and send the error through the channel.
A channel carries values, not failures: without an error field in the result struct (or errgroup) the failure of the call is dropped.
Goroutines are cheap but not free and not bounded: one per request without a semaphore or worker limit turns overload into memory pressure and scheduler latency.
Closing a channel that senders still use panics; ownership of close belongs to the sender, and the convention must be documented at the async entry point.
